title: The One Who Stayed
subtitle: The Legend of Master Genkai
teaser: A hundred disciples went down to hold the bridge at Ume, and their teacher was ordered to stay behind and keep the lamps lit. Forty years later, he walked to the warlord’s castle with his fists closed.

sections.heading: I. The Bridge at Ume
paragraphs: Master Genkai counted his students every morning, the way a farmer counts goats. Every morning there were a hundred.

Kōzan temple sat at the top of a long stone stair above the river. Its granary fed three valleys in a bad year, and its monks learned the open hand from Genkai: no fists, no blades, only the palm, which breaks a man’s guard, then his footing, and leaves the rest of him alone.
“The fist takes,” he told every new disciple. “The open hand puts a man on the ground and lets him keep his teeth. Most of them are grateful afterwards.”

He was forty, and the hardest teacher in the east. He never learned their names. He called them by their faults: Crooked Elbow, Late Again, Talks Too Much. When the abbot asked why, Genkai said, “If I learn their names, I will have favourites. I have no favourites. I dislike them all equally.”
He had one rule of manners. “Before you put a man down, tell him your name. It is only polite. He may wish to complain later.”
In the famine year, the warlord Oda Kurogane marched for the grain with eight thousand hungry men. The only road to Kōzan crossed the river at Ume, on a bridge of black pine three men wide.
The hundred went down at dawn. Genkai tied back his sleeves to go with them, and the abbot met him at the top of the stair.
“You’ll stay,” said the abbot. “Keep the lamps lit.”
“Give the lamps to a novice.”
“I’m giving them to you. They are going down to hold the bridge, Genkai. You would go down to win it.”

Genkai did not understand, and was too angry to try. He stood at the top of the stair and counted them out. A hundred. Crooked Elbow, passing, said, “Don’t worry, Master. We’ll keep our elbows in.” Genkai told him to keep his chin up as well.

They held the bridge at Ume from dawn until sunset. From the temple, Genkai could hear it all day: not the ring of steel, but a dull, steady beating, like flails on a threshing floor. He trimmed the wicks. He topped up the oil. At sunset the sound stopped.
That night the rains came, the river rose over the bridge, and Kurogane, a day late, turned his army around. The grain was saved.
None of the hundred came back.

sections.heading: II. Forty Years at the Post
paragraphs: Kurogane took the bodies with him. He paid his soldiers by the head, and he was a careful man with money.

His army went home with its wounded piled in the carts it had brought for Kōzan’s rice: broken arms, broken knees, men fished out of the river downstream. Hardly any dead. The open hand was never meant to kill.

The night before the battle, the abbot had burned the temple register so the warlord could not trace the disciples to their villages and hang their fathers. When Genkai sat down to paint a hundred memorial tablets, he had nothing to paint.

He had a hundred faults. Crooked Elbow. Late Again. Talks Too Much. Drops His Guard. Breathes Like a Bellows. He sat before the blank tablets until the lamp guttered out. Then he went into the courtyard and hit the cedar post with a closed fist until his knuckles split.
He did not stop for forty years.

He unlearned the open hand and learned the other kind: the throat, the temple, the soft place under the ear, the blow that leaves a man nothing to be grateful for. He struck the post ten thousand times a day, and every few years wore through it and dragged in another. His knuckles grew thick and pale as knots in pine, and the younger monks walked the long way round the courtyard.
He kept the lamps lit. Nobody else went near them, because he was usually standing beside them.
In his sixty-first year, word came up the stair that Oda Kurogane had died in bed of a fever, with a priest holding his hand.
Genkai took it personally.
“He had no right,” he told the new abbot. “I wasn’t ready.”
“Then perhaps it’s finished,” said the abbot hopefully.
“He has a son,” said Genkai, and went back to the post.
He trained nineteen more years. At eighty he tied back his sleeves and walked down the stair for the first time since the morning he counted them out.

sections.heading: III. Sixty Men
paragraphs: The bridge at Ume had been rebuilt in stone. Nothing on it showed what had happened there, not even a stain. Genkai stood in the middle for a long time, then crossed.
Kurogane’s castle stood two days east, on a black rock above the plain. The old warlord had named it after himself, being that kind of man. His son, Lord Oda Sadamune, kept sixty soldiers in it.
At a teahouse below the walls, the owner looked at the old monk’s knuckles and asked where he was going.
“To kill a man.”
The owner took in the white brows, the bent back, the beads. “At your age?”
“I would have come sooner,” said Genkai. “I was practising.”

He walked up to the gate at moonrise. The first guard laughed at him. Genkai put a palm under the man’s chin and laid him down in the gateway like a dropped coat. The second came with a spear. Genkai stepped inside the point, took the shaft, and returned it across the man’s shins. Then the alarm bell rang, and the rest came.

He went through two yards and up the stairs of the keep. They came at him with spears, swords, a chain, and once, in the kitchens, a ladle. He broke their guard, then their footing. He turned wrists, folded knees, sent elbows the wrong way, never hurrying, like a man sweeping a floor he had swept ten thousand times. One big sergeant in good armour went backwards through a paper screen into the room where the lord’s accountants slept.
Sixty men came at him that night, and sixty went down. Not one of them died.

He told himself they were not worth the trouble, that he was saving his fist for the son. But for forty years he had trained that hand to close, and in the yards it kept opening, as if it had been open longer and remembered.

sections.heading: IV. The Book
paragraphs: A lamp was burning by the bed in the lord’s chamber. Sadamune was perhaps thirty. He met Genkai in his sleeping robe with his father’s sword, and he held it well. Genkai took it from him anyway, swept his feet, knelt on his chest and raised a fist over his throat.
Sadamune did not beg. He looked up at the white brows and the white knuckles, and seemed to recognise them.
“My father said one of you would come,” he said. “He counted the heads from the bridge. A hundred. He said Kōzan had a hundred and one, and the one who stayed home was the one to worry about.”
The fist stayed where it was.
“He kept a guard on his door for twenty years,” said Sadamune. “I suppose it’s my turn.”
Forty years of blank tablets, split knuckles and cedar posts worn through. All of it had been for this one blow, and he had practised it more times than there were grains in Kōzan’s granary.

Then he heard it again, the dull beating from the bridge. A hundred of his students had held Ume all day against eight thousand men, and not one of them had killed anybody. He had taught them not to. He had outlived every one of them, and walked two days to be the first man of Kōzan to kill.
They had gone down to hold the bridge. He had come to win it. The abbot had seen that forty years ago.
Genkai opened his hand. He laid it flat on the young lord’s chest and pressed once, so Sadamune would feel how easily it could have gone the other way.
“Your father counted everything,” he said. “Did he write down their names?”

“They gave them,” Sadamune said slowly. “Every one. The clerks thought it was madness, monks shouting their names at the men they were throwing in the river. They wrote it all in the head-book. The name, the soldier who took the head, the price paid.”
Tell him your name. It is only polite.
“Fetch it,” said Genkai. “Then a clean book. Copy out their names in your own hand. Not the soldiers. Not the prices. Only the names.”
Sadamune wrote all night while sixty men groaned in the yards below. Genkai sat by the door and kept the lamp trimmed.

At dawn Sadamune gave him a hundred names. Genkai read them slowly. Crooked Elbow had been called Sōshin. Late Again had been Ekan. Talks Too Much had taken the temple name Mokuzen, which means Silent Meditation.
Genkai laughed out loud, alone in a dead warlord’s castle, for the first time in forty years.
“That’s all?” said Sadamune. “You came through sixty men for a list?”
“I came through sixty men to kill you,” said Genkai, tucking the book into his robe. “The list was an afterthought. Hire better guards.”

sections.heading: V. The Last Teacher
paragraphs: He carried the book home and took a mallet and chisel to the temple stair.
He cut one name into each of the top hundred steps, and it took him a year. The abbot asked why steps, and not a wall.
“People walk past a wall,” said Genkai. “They have to use a step.”
Above the hundredth there is one more step, still blank. The abbot assumes it is for Genkai. Genkai says it is for a broom.

When he is not trimming the lamps, he is in the duelling rings. Nobody is sure what he wants there. Not money: his winnings go up the stair for lamp oil. Not glory: he has outlived everyone who would have cared. Some say he is waiting for someone good enough to put him on that last step. If so, he is very hard to please.

He fights the way he taught. His fists are wrapped in old cloth over the knuckles he ruined on the cedar posts, bound tight so they remember to stay open. He strikes with the palm. He finds your faults and corrects them one at a time, a dropped elbow, a lifted heel, a chin that should be up, until your guard is gone and your footing with it. Fighters who have lost to him say it is like being lectured by a landslide. He almost never kills, and the ring-masters complain it is bad for business.

The rings are full of the young and the brave, who have come to die famous. He puts them on the ground with their teeth in and sends them home with a list of their faults. Most of them are grateful afterwards.

Every morning, before the lamps, he counts his prayer beads the way a farmer counts goats. Sōshin, Crooked Elbow. Ekan, Late Again. Mokuzen, Talks Too Much. A name and a fault for every bead, because they were both. Every morning there are a hundred.
Then he goes down to the ring, looks out from under those heavy white brows at whoever has come to try him, and raises one open hand.
“I have outlived braver men,” he says. “Come.”

quote: I have outlived braver men. Come.
